title: Composition of Body Fluids and Compartments

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with persistent vomiting and diarrhea has labs showing elevated BUN. The intern asks why his measured serum osmolality is high but the patient does not appear to have shrunken cells on biopsy. Which property of urea best explains this observation?
choices: It is actively transported into cells
It is filtered but not reabsorbed
explanations: Incorrect. Protein binding does not explain its osmotic ineffectiveness.
Correct. Urea is an ineffective osmole because it freely crosses cell membranes; it raises measured osmolality but not tonicity, so cells do not shrink.
Incorrect. Active uptake is not the basis for its lack of tonicity effect.
Incorrect. Renal handling does not determine cellular tonicity effect.
Incorrect. Oncotic pressure is the role of plasma proteins, not urea.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman develops severe diarrhea with significant loss of isotonic fluid. Which fluid compartment changes are most expected?
explanations: Incorrect. Isotonic loss does not directly reduce ICF, since tonicity is unchanged.
Correct. Isotonic fluid loss reduces ECF volume only; without a tonicity change, water does not shift between compartments and ICF remains normal.
Incorrect. ECF decreases, not increases, with isotonic fluid loss.
Incorrect. ECF decreases, not increases, with diarrhea.
Incorrect. ICF is not increased after isotonic dehydration.

questions.stem: Which solute will NOT cause water movement across cell membranes?
explanations: Incorrect. Albumin contributes to oncotic pressure across vascular membranes.
Correct. BUN (urea) freely crosses cell membranes and is an ineffective osmole, so it does not cause sustained water shifts.
Incorrect. Glucose is an effective osmole and shifts water in hyperglycemia.
Incorrect. Mannitol is an effective osmole used therapeutically.
Incorrect. Sodium is the principal effective osmole of the ECF.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman with chronic hyponatremia (Na+ 118 mEq/L) develops seizures in the ED. Which initial fluid therapy is most appropriate?
explanations: Incorrect. Hypotonic saline would worsen hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Isotonic saline corrects sodium too slowly and inadequately for active seizures.
Correct. 3% hypertonic saline is used to rapidly raise serum sodium and reduce cerebral edema in symptomatic severe hyponatremia.
Incorrect. D5W after metabolism becomes free water and worsens hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Lactated Ringer's is isotonic and not preferred for symptomatic seizures from hyponatremia.

questions.stem: In a Darrow-Yannet diagram, the height of each compartment box represents:
explanations: Incorrect. Width represents volume, not height.
Incorrect. Permeability is not depicted.
Incorrect. Oncotic pressure is not the axis.
Correct. In Darrow-Yannet diagrams, height represents osmolality and width represents volume.
Incorrect. Total solute amount is depicted by area, not height.

questions.stem: Which best defines tonicity in clinical fluid balance?
choices: Concentration of solutes that cannot freely cross membranes
Includes urea and other freely diffusible solutes
Sum of all solutes regardless of membrane behavior
explanations: Correct. Tonicity is the concentration of effective osmoles — solutes that cannot freely cross cell membranes.
Incorrect. Tonicity excludes urea, which freely crosses membranes.
Incorrect. Oncotic pressure is a different concept relevant to capillary-interstitial fluid balance.
Incorrect. That describes osmolality, not tonicity.
Incorrect. Osmolality measures all particles; tonicity only includes effective osmoles.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes insipidus develops loss of pure free water. Compared with normal, the expected compartment changes are:
choices: Hypertonic ECF, water shifts ICF → ECF
Hypotonic ECF, water shifts ECF → ICF
explanations: Correct. Loss of free water concentrates ECF solutes, making ECF hypertonic; water shifts from ICF to ECF, causing cellular dehydration.
Incorrect. Loss of free water raises, not lowers, ECF tonicity.
Incorrect. Pure water loss is not isotonic.
Incorrect. Water loss reduces total volume; not an isotonic expansion.
Incorrect. Tonicity rises with free water loss.

questions.stem: After bolus administration of D5W (after glucose metabolism), what is the expected compartment effect?
explanations: Correct. After glucose metabolism, D5W functions as free water, distributing throughout total body water and expanding both ECF and ICF.
Incorrect. ICF also expands when free water is added.
Incorrect. ECF does not decrease; both compartments expand.
Incorrect. ICF expands, not decreases, with hypotonic fluid administration.
Incorrect. There is volume change in both compartments.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with diabetic ketoacidosis presents with profoundly elevated glucose. Which mechanism best describes the expected fluid shift?
explanations: Correct. Hyperglycemia makes ECF hypertonic, drawing water from ICF; osmotic diuresis then causes loss of water and electrolytes from both compartments.
Incorrect. ECF becomes hypertonic, not hypotonic, in hyperglycemia.
Incorrect. Hyperglycemia is not isotonic.
Incorrect. The shift is principally driven by glucose, not selective potassium-water shifts.
Incorrect. Sodium retention does not describe DKA fluid dynamics.

questions.stem: Approximately how does an isotonic fluid bolus of 0.9% NaCl distribute within the ECF, in plasma versus interstitium?
choices: Variable, dependent on patient body weight
explanations: Incorrect. Only about a quarter remains in the plasma.
Correct. About 25% remains in plasma and 75% goes to interstitial fluid, following the normal ECF distribution ratio.
Incorrect. The distribution is not equal between plasma and interstitium.
Incorrect. The distribution favors interstitium, not plasma.
Incorrect. The distribution ratio cited is general, not principally weight-dependent in this brick.

questions.stem: A patient receives a large infusion of 0.9% NaCl. Which complication is the brick specifically warning about with normal saline?
explanations: Incorrect. Cerebral edema is the concern with hypotonic, not isotonic, saline.
Incorrect. Hypercalcemia is not a typical NS complication.
Correct. Large volumes of normal saline can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis or fluid overload.
Incorrect. Lactic acidosis is not the concern with NS.
Incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is not a recognized NS complication.

questions.stem: Why is rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia particularly dangerous?
explanations: Incorrect. Cerebral edema is the risk in rapid correction of hypernatremia, not hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Acidosis is not the main risk emphasized.
Correct. Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome.
Incorrect. Hyperkalemia is not the central risk highlighted.
Incorrect. Thrombophlebitis is associated with hypertonic fluids in peripheral lines, not chronic hyponatremia correction itself.

questions.stem: Which compartments contain most of the body's total water?
explanations: Incorrect. Fat and muscle are tissue types, not water compartments.
Incorrect. While interstitial fluid is part of ECF, this answer omits ICF.
Correct. The body's total water is distributed primarily between intracellular fluid (ICF) and extracellular fluid (ECF).
Incorrect. Plasma and interstitial fluid are subdivisions of the ECF, not the principal split.
Incorrect. Transcellular fluid is a small ECF compartment.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man drinks excessive water rapidly. Which best describes the expected compartment effect?
choices: ECF becomes hypertonic, water shifts ICF → ECF
ECF becomes hypotonic, water shifts ECF → ICF
explanations: Incorrect. Excess water dilutes ECF; tonicity decreases, not increases.
Correct. Excessive free water dilutes ECF making it hypotonic, driving water into cells (especially dangerous in brain tissue).
Incorrect. ICF expands, not contracts.
Incorrect. ECF expands, not contracts, with water intoxication.
Incorrect. The water enters both ECF and ICF.

questions.stem: Lactated Ringer's solution differs from 0.9% NaCl by:
explanations: Incorrect. LR is isotonic.
Correct. Lactated Ringer's is a balanced crystalloid containing lactate as a buffer and physiologic concentrations of electrolytes.
Incorrect. LR does not contain dextrose.
Incorrect. LR contains sodium (~130 mEq/L).
Incorrect. LR is isotonic; it does not provide free water.

questions.stem: Which clinical situation is matched correctly with its compartment effect?
explanations: Incorrect. Hemorrhage is isotonic loss, not hypotonic expansion.
Incorrect. Hyperglycemia produces hypertonic ECF.
Correct. Hypernatremia produces hypertonic ECF, drawing water from ICF and causing cellular contraction.
Incorrect. SIADH produces hypotonic, not hypertonic, ECF.
Incorrect. Water intoxication produces hypotonic ECF.

questions.stem: Which calculated value is used to estimate serum osmolality?
explanations: Incorrect. Chloride is not used in the standard osmolality estimation.
Incorrect. Sodium, not potassium, is the major contributor.
Incorrect. Albumin is not in the osmolality formula.
Correct. Estimated serum osmolality = 2 × [Na+] + [Glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate and other ions are not used in this estimation.

questions.stem: A young man with severe traumatic brain injury and elevated ICP is given 20% mannitol. Which compartment effect drives its therapeutic action?
choices: Increases ECF tonicity, draws water from ICF → ECF
explanations: Incorrect. Mannitol shrinks, not swells, brain cells.
Correct. Mannitol raises ECF osmolality (effective osmole), drawing water out of intracranial cells into ECF.
Incorrect. Mannitol is hypertonic, not isotonic.
Incorrect. Mannitol is not a plasma protein.
Incorrect. The fluid shift is water, not selective potassium.

questions.stem: What happens to fluid compartments after hypotonic fluid administration?
explanations: Correct. Hypotonic fluid distributes through total body water, expanding both ECF and ICF.
Incorrect. ICF also expands.
Incorrect. ICF expands, not decreases.
Incorrect. There is volume change.
Incorrect. Both compartments expand, not just ICF.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on 3% NaCl infusion is at greatest risk of which complication if his sodium rises too quickly?
explanations: Incorrect. Cerebral edema is the risk with hypotonic infusions.
Incorrect. Hyperchloremic acidosis is more associated with normal saline overload.
Incorrect. Hypocalcemic tetany is not the central risk in this scenario.
Correct. Rapid correction of sodium with hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination syndrome.
Incorrect. Pulmonary fibrosis is not a recognized hypertonic saline complication.

questions.stem: A patient with sepsis-induced hypovolemia is being resuscitated. The clinician chooses isotonic crystalloid. Which compartment effect is intended?
choices: Pure shift of water from ICF to ECF
explanations: Correct. Isotonic crystalloid expands ECF (both intravascular and interstitial) without affecting ICF volume, supporting circulation.
Incorrect. Isotonic fluids do not preferentially expand ICF.
Incorrect. Free water replacement is the role of hypotonic fluids.
Incorrect. Isotonic fluids do not shift water between ICF and ECF.
Incorrect. Cell shrinkage is the action of hypertonic fluid.

questions.stem: Which solute is normally the principal effective osmole determining ECF tonicity?
explanations: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is not the principal tonicity determinant.
Incorrect. Calcium does not determine plasma tonicity.
Incorrect. Glucose contributes only at high concentrations.
Incorrect. Potassium is principally intracellular.
Correct. Sodium is the primary determinant of ECF tonicity; alterations in serum sodium are the most common cause of clinically significant tonicity changes.

questions.stem: A regulatory volume increase (RVI) and regulatory volume decrease (RVD) describe which cellular phenomenon?
explanations: Incorrect. Transcellular pumping is not the described mechanism.
Correct. RVI and RVD involve transport of ions and organic osmolytes to adjust intracellular tonicity and restore normal cell volume.
Incorrect. Apoptosis is not the mechanism.
Incorrect. Cells do not pump water directly with ATP.
Incorrect. Lipid raft formation is unrelated to volume regulation.

questions.stem: Which solute can become a clinically important effective osmole in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)?
explanations: Incorrect. Albumin is an oncotic, not osmotic, contributor.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate is not the principal osmole here.
Correct. Markedly elevated glucose acts as an effective osmole, drawing water from ICF to ECF in HHS and DKA.
Incorrect. Sodium is normally the principal osmole, but in HHS the dramatic shift is driven by glucose.
Incorrect. Urea is an ineffective osmole.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with prolonged vomiting/diarrhea, confusion, and abnormal sodium and glucose levels has lost ECF volume. The MOST appropriate INITIAL fluid is:
explanations: Incorrect. Hypotonic saline does not adequately restore ECF volume.
Correct. Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% NaCl or Lactated Ringer's) restores ECF volume in patients with isotonic-leaning losses; rate and ongoing electrolyte correction follow.
Incorrect. Mannitol is reserved for elevated ICP.
Incorrect. 3% hypertonic saline is reserved for severely symptomatic hyponatremia.
Incorrect. D5W is hypotonic after metabolism and not appropriate for initial volume restoration.
